sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: Title page and abstract of Dusengumuremyi's single-author paper on an AI-mediated RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) matrix in organisational boardrooms, with the author's affiliation at Southern Federal University and contact details. The background asks why organisations, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, end up with what the text calls 97.4% input-output misalignment, 99.6% operational inefficiency, 92.4% risk non-detection and $14.3 million in losses. The method is a qualitative case study based on the author's own professional experience in an anonymised organisation, comparing a human-mediated RACI with an AI-augmented one over 24 months, with 1,247 decision events and 89 strategic meetings. The stated results are 97.4%, 99.6%, 99.1% and 92.4% on four measures, and the paper concludes that AI-mediated RACI is mandatory for developing economies. The same four figures appear in the abstract both as problems and as achievements, and the highlights repeat them.

sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Introduction and the start of the theoretical background. The paper claims a gap: no study has integrated the RACI framework with machine-learning sensemaking for pre-emptive risk closure. The author bases the work on their own experience in a multinational organisation in a sub-Saharan African market, observed during a master's programme in the Russian Federation, and says the wider region had not adopted even a manual RACI. Five research objectives are listed: to conceptualise the AI-mediated RACI, compare it empirically with the human-mediated one, quantify its effect on organisational defensibility, give a mandatory protocol for international business firms, and an outline of the paper. Section 2.1 describes the RACI matrix's four roles and argues its static nature creates "vulnerability gates".

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Theoretical background and the start of the methodology. The paper cites literature on a "RACI gap" and on sensemaking (Weick), argues AI removes interpretive latency and bias, and states three propositions: AI-mediated RACI reduces decision-to-action latency (P1), achieves near-zero accountability-tracking errors (P2), and detects over 75% of vulnerability gates before they occur (P3). It defines "organisational defensibility" as ex-ante risk closure, citing the author's own work under review, and calls sub-Saharan organisations' governance a "shameful stage". Section 3 describes a single revelatory case study in an anonymised multinational in high-complexity logistics and infrastructure across four countries, where the author worked 36 months (2021–2024) plus 12 months of observation. Phase 1 (months 1–12) is the human-mediated baseline: 647 decisions and 42 meetings.

summary.text: Remaining implementation phases, the measurement table, findings and the start of the discussion. Phases 2–4 are AI system design (an LLM architecture with real-time APIs), implementation, and observation (600 decisions, 47 meetings). The table compares baseline and AI: decision-to-action latency 94.2 h (SD 31.4) against 5.0 h (SD 2.1); accountability error rate 22.7% against 0.9%; escalations per decision 0.84 against 0.11; ex-ante vulnerability detection 12.3% against 78.4%; defensibility score 31.4 against 94.2. Findings: a 94.7% latency reduction (t(1245) = 47.3, p < .001), 99.1% accountability accuracy against 77.3%, 78.4% detection, and $14.3M avoided losses with 387% ROI over 24 months. A comparison with 12 peer organisations leads to a five-phase "mandatory implementation protocol". The 78.4% detection figure here differs from the 92.4% in the abstract.

summary.text: Discussion, conclusions and end matter. The paper claims three contributions and argues that institutional voids are self-perpetuated by the absence of structured accountability tools, presenting AI-mediated RACI as a technology leapfrog. It lists three limitations: a single case, the author's insider role, and dependence on data quality. Managerial implications call human-only RACI no longer defensible. The conclusion cites 48 months of case evidence, a 94.7% latency reduction, 99.1% accountability accuracy and over 78% detection. Acknowledgments, a no-conflicts statement, a no-funding statement, and a data-availability statement follow. The last says the data come from the author's field experience and secondary sources and that no new datasets were generated or analysed, which sits uneasily with the decision counts reported earlier.
